Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Title: Diagnosis
Details: The failing test opens a 7z archive whose header is itself compressed (kEncodedHeader) using LZMA2 with a non-default dictionary size (the reported case is 16 MB).

Here’s how the failure unfolds step-by-step:

1) SevenZFile construction
- SevenZFile(File) delegates to SevenZFile(File, byte[]).
- The constructor calls readHeaders(password).

2) Header parsing and detection of encoded header
- readHeaders reads the initial NextHeader.
- It detects that the header is encoded (nid == NID.kEncodedHeader) and calls readEncodedHeader.

3) Decoding the encoded header
- readEncodedHeader builds a decoder stack from the first folder in the archive:
  - For each coder in the folder, Coders.addDecoder is used to create the appropriate decoder.
  - For an LZMA2-coded header, this goes into LZMA2Decoder.decode.

4) LZMA2 dictionary size derivation
- LZMA2Decoder.decode interprets coder.properties[0] to compute the dictionary size using the standard LZMA2 formula:
  - For the given file, this yields a 16 MB dictionary (16,777,216 bytes).
  - It then constructs a new LZMA2InputStream(in, dictionarySize).

5) Failure due to overly strict dictionary limit
- The thrown exception reported by the issue (“16 MB dictionary is too big”) indicates that LZMA2InputStream imposes an artificial upper limit on the dictionary size that is below 16 MB (commonly 8 MB in earlier implementations).
- This contradicts the LZMA2 specification and the code in LZMA2Decoder that explicitly allows dictionary sizes up to 4 GiB (it guards only against sizes > 4 GiB).
- As a result, when trying to decode the encoded header with a 16 MB dictionary, LZMA2InputStream rejects the size and throws, causing SevenZFile construction to fail.

Why this matches the bug report and test:
- The issue summary (“7z: 16 MB dictionary is too big”) matches exactly the behavior when an internal check caps the dictionary lower than the value used by 7-Zip defaults (16 MB).
- The test name testCompressedHeaderWithNonDefaultDictionarySize confirms it is exercising the encoded-header path with a larger-than-default dictionary.

Root cause:
- An unnecessarily strict maximum dictionary size check inside the LZMA2 input stream implementation rejects valid LZMA2 dictionaries (e.g., 16 MB) when decoding encoded headers.
- All upstream steps (reading the header, identifying the coder, computing the dictionary size) are correct; the failure is triggered by the LZMA2InputStream constructor or validation logic that enforces too small a maximum.

Consequences:
- Opening 7z archives (especially those with encoded headers) created with standard 7-Zip settings using a 16 MB dictionary fails, even though the archive is valid per the LZMA2 spec.

Recommendation:
- Relax or remove the low cap in the LZMA2InputStream dictionary size validation to accept at least 16 MB (and ideally up to the LZMA2-specified maximum of 4 GiB, with practical memory considerations). This will allow decoding of encoded headers with larger dictionaries and make the behavior consistent with LZMA2Decoder’s computation and the LZMA2 specification.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
